definition: Inflate means to increase something beyond its true or proper amount.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inflate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inflate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The two organizers each inflated their crowd counts until the two rallies, by their own arithmetic, outnumbered the city.
Overstating stretches the truth a size or two; inflating pumps it well past its proper amount — the difference between 'a strong turnout' and doubling the count.
Falsify sits past inflate: an inflated figure at least began as a real one, while a falsified figure walks away from the truth altogether.

Exaggerate stretches something real in the telling — the fish gets longer, the traffic worse, the crowd rowdier — and it works on anything a story can hold. Inflate does its stretching to amounts: a figure, a price, a total pumped past its true size, usually on paper.

Pad means to bulk something out with filler that adds nothing real — extra pages in a report, invented hours on a timesheet. Inflate keeps the same dishonesty but swells the number itself instead of stuffing material in around it. Padding adds bulk; inflating feeds a figure air.

Inflate means to increase something beyond its true or proper amount.
The cottage listing said 'nearly 1,200 square feet.' The tape measure said 900 — the listing had inflated the number by counting the porch, the toolshed, and a crawlspace no adult could stand up in.
Nothing was invented; a true figure had simply been pumped up until it read half again its size.
Inflate is the precise verb because the trick runs in one direction and works on amounts.
The root means 'to blow into': the listing blew air into 900 until it looked like 1,200.
Lying invents; inflating takes a real number, price, or claim and swells it past its proper size.
Inflate is the verb of crooked arithmetic: figures, prices, titles, and claims pumped past their true amount, usually by someone with something to gain.
Magnify, its unit-mate, distorts how big a thing appears without touching the books; amplify strengthens something real; intensify says the degree itself rose.
When a number has been fed air, inflate is the accusation.

When the great exposition closed in October 1893, its promoters wired the newspapers a triumphant total: twenty-seven million visitors had passed through the gates.
Historians who later pulled the turnstile ledgers found a quieter story.
Daily counts had been copied upward before release, and complimentary passes were counted twice.
The organizers had inflated the attendance, and not modestly: the audited total came to barely twenty-one million paid admissions.
Investors were watching, and a fair that drew twenty-seven million could borrow against its glory; one that drew twenty-one million could not.
The habit outlived the fair.
Wherever a number carries money or pride on its back, someone will be tempted to pump it past the truth -- and someone else will have to pull the ledgers.
